name: Deep-set vs wide-set eye spacing

card.summary: A framework for judging how far apart the eyes sit and how deeply they sit in the sockets, used to decide which hairstyles, brow work, makeup and eyewear flatter the eye area.
card.aka: eye spacing; close-set eyes; interocular distance
card.note: Surgical changes to eye spacing (orbital osteotomy) are major craniofacial operations.

quick.overview:
Eye spacing describes how far apart the eyes are relative to the face, and eye set describes how deep they sit in the sockets. Looksmaxxing forums treat both as part of the eye area, often using ratios such as inter-canthal or interpupillary distance compared with eye width or face width.
People use the framework to decide where to concentrate effort: eyebrow shape, eyeliner and lash placement, glasses, hairstyle and, for a few, surgery. Published medical sources define extreme spacing (hypertelorism) and describe surgical correction of it, but they do not set an attractiveness standard.
quick.how: In practice people measure or eyeball their spacing from front-facing photos, compare it with a ratio they prefer, and then adjust the visual impression: brows that start closer to or further from the nose, eyeliner extended or concentrated at the inner corner, frames with a bridge that visually widens or narrows the gap, and lighter or darker eye makeup. A smaller group discusses bone-level options such as orbital surgery or palate expansion.
quick.risks: Everyday styling changes carry little risk. Orbital box osteotomy and facial bipartition are major craniofacial operations; medical sources list bleeding, infection, cerebrospinal fluid leaks, vision problems and canthal drift among possible complications. Forum members also note that fixating on small ratio differences can become distressing.

lead: Eye spacing is the distance between the eyes, and eye set is how deep or prominent they sit within the orbits. In looksmaxxing discussion, eyes are described as close-set, average or wide-set, and as deep-set or protruding, and these descriptors are treated as part of the eye area's overall impression [1][2].

The payoff is mostly in styling and framing. People use their assessment of spacing and set to choose brow shape and length, eyeliner and shadow placement, lash emphasis, eyewear and hairstyles that make the eye area read as balanced, and a smaller number ask about surgical or orthodontic routes [3][4][12]. Cosmetic brands publish the same kind of advice, for example keeping the inner corners light and extending the brow tail for close-set eyes [12].

Research on the topic comes from two directions. Perception studies have asked which interocular proportions people rate as most attractive on computer-manipulated faces, with one 2010 study placing the preferred ratio at about 46 percent of face width [10]. Clinical sources define abnormal spacing (hypertelorism and hypotelorism) and describe surgical correction in craniofacial conditions [5][13].

chain: Measure or assess eye spacing and eye set
Choose brows, liner, eyewear and hair to balance the eye area
More harmonious-looking eyes in photos and in person
angle.text: Knowing whether the eyes sit close, average or wide lets people pick brow shapes, liner placement and frames that shift how the gap reads. A few go further and discuss orbital or palate procedures, which change structure rather than appearance cues.

paras: Eye spacing is usually assessed from a front-facing photograph. Forum members compare the distance between the eyes with the width of one eye, with the face width at the cheekbones, or with the distance from pupils to lips, and label the result close-set, balanced or wide-set [1][2][16]. A commonly repeated rule of thumb, also used by makeup brands, is that if the gap between the inner corners is narrower than the width of one eye, the eyes are close-set [12].

Eye set is a separate, depth-based idea: deep-set eyes sit further back under the brow ridge, while shallow or prominent eyes sit closer to the front plane of the face. Makeup educators describe deep-set eyes as a matter of position in the socket rather than eye shape, with the brow bone appearing stronger and shading the lid [12]. In medicine, posterior displacement of the eyeball within the orbit has its own name, enophthalmos, which is listed with causes such as orbital trauma and certain syndromes; the clinical term refers to displacement outside the normal range, not to ordinary deep-set eyes [14].

Interpupillary distance (IPD) is the measurement opticians use for lens centring. A 2012 US Army survey cited on Wikipedia found mean distance IPD of 64.0 mm in men (range 53.0 to 77.0 mm) and 61.7 mm in women (range 51.0 to 74.5 mm) [9]. Forum threads more often use ratios: the eye spacing ratio (ESR), the inter-canthal distance relative to palpebral fissure length (ICD:PFL), and IPD relative to bizygomatic width [1][16].

Related terms include telecanthus (only the inner corners are further apart), and epicanthic folds, vertical skin folds at the inner corner that are common in many East and Southeast Asian populations and can change how wide the inner gap looks [5][15].

The best-known perception study is Pallett, Link and Lee (Vision Research, 2010). Participants made paired attractiveness comparisons between faces that differed only in spacing. In four experiments with 20 to 42 students each, faces rated most attractive had an eye-to-mouth distance of about 36 to 37 percent of face length and an interocular distance of about 46 percent of face width, matching the averages measured on 40 female faces. The authors noted that only mostly Caucasian female faces were tested [10].

A 2026 arXiv preprint from Marburg University repeated the width-ratio approach on male faces drawn from the Chicago Face Database. With 97 participants and 14,542 pairwise comparisons, it estimated optimal width ratios between roughly 0.458 and 0.472 and interpreted the results as consistent with a preference for averageness; the authors said no single universal optimum could be determined, and the work has not been peer-reviewed [11].

Posts about close-set eyes frequently ask for non-surgical changes. Suggestions that appear include eyebrow shaping, eyeliner placed toward the outer corners, lighter makeup rather than dark tones around the inner corner, and eyewear [3][7][18]. Other threads ask whether orbital procedures or palate expansion could alter spacing, and some ask for non-surgical alternatives specifically [4][17]. Members sometimes reference the 'OBO' procedure, an orbital box osteotomy, as the structural option [3][4].

One widely read thread argues that spacing ratios are 'misunderstood' and over-weighted, offering a broader assessment of eye-area pleasantness and using a well-known actor with a low ratio as a case study of other features compensating [1]. Another asks whether there are attractive men with close-set eyes at all [19], and a further thread compares wide-set and close-set examples [6]. Some posters describe worry about spacing as distressing, with at least one thread asking whether the concern reflects body dysmorphia [20].

Beauty-industry guidance for close-set eyes, as published by L'Oreal Paris, advises keeping inner corners light and open, starting liner away from the inner corner, shading lighter at the inner corner and deeper at the outer, and lengthening the brow tail slightly beyond its natural end while keeping the inner brow soft [12]. Forum members describe similar ideas, along with picking glasses and hairstyles that add width at the temples [7][18].

Makeup educators also describe adapting shadow placement to deep-set eyes so colour stays visible below a prominent brow bone [12]. Proponents of these approaches regard them as reversible and low-cost ways to change the visual impression.

Hypertelorism is an abnormally increased distance between the eyes and is a feature of many congenital conditions, including Apert, Crouzon and Noonan syndromes. Correction is usually done between ages 5 and 8, using box osteotomy (first performed by Paul Tessier) or facial bipartition (developed by Jacques van der Meulen in the 1970s) [5]. Complications listed include bleeding, infection, cerebrospinal fluid leak, double vision and canthal drift, which is hard to correct [5].

Hypotelorism, abnormally close orbits, is associated with conditions such as trisomy 13 and holoprosencephaly [13]. These sources describe medical conditions, not cosmetic preferences, and the surgeries are designed to narrow, not widen, spacing.

No studies found. Medical literature on eye spacing concerns genetic syndromes and craniofacial surgery. Separately, perception experiments on computer-manipulated faces have examined which proportions raters prefer [10][11].

timeline.event: Jacques van der Meulen develops facial bipartition, a technique for correcting hypertelorism, building on Paul Tessier's box osteotomy [5].

Pallett, Link and Lee report that an interocular distance of about 46 percent of face width and an eye-to-mouth distance of about 36 percent of face length were rated most attractive on female faces [10].
A US Army anthropometric survey records mean IPD of 64.0 mm in men and 61.7 mm in women [9].
A preprint testing width ratios on male faces estimates optimal values of roughly 0.46 to 0.47 [11].

lore.intro: Eye spacing is a recurring topic on looksmax.org, with threads on ratios, celebrity comparisons and ways to change the look [1][2][6].

claims.claim: Close-set eyes are a major attractiveness factor that is hard to fix
claims.believers: Posters describe close-set eyes as a defining feature of the upper face and ask what can change it [4][3].
claims.experts: No published study sets an optimal spacing for attractiveness for individuals; a 2010 experiment found the most-preferred interocular ratio matched the average of 0.46 for female faces [10].

claims.claim: Spacing ratios are over-weighted and a holistic view works better
claims.believers: A thread author argues that ESR and similar ratios distort assessment and suggests a different measure of the eye area [1].
claims.experts: No published trial compares ratio-based and holistic methods; the perception studies test spacing on its own with other features held constant [10][11].

claims.claim: Dark eye colour or dark makeup makes close-set eyes look closer
claims.believers: A thread states that close-set eyes should not also be dark-coloured [8].
claims.experts: Makeup guidance from L'Oreal Paris likewise advises avoiding dark liner or shadow near the inner corner for close-set eyes; no published studies have tested eye colour specifically [12].

claims.claim: Orbital surgery or palate expansion can change eye spacing
claims.believers: Members ask whether such procedures could widen the set of the eyes [3][4][17].
claims.experts: Surgical hypertelorism correction narrows widely spaced eyes in children with a medical condition and is a major operation with listed risks [5].

claims.claim: Eyebrows, liner and glasses can visually widen close-set eyes
claims.believers: Forum members and makeup brands describe lengthening the brow tail, lining the outer half of the lid and choosing frames that add width [7][12][18].
claims.experts: No published studies have measured how these techniques change perceived spacing.

claims.believers: Threads quote ESR and ICD:PFL benchmarks and compare faces against them [1][16].
claims.experts: Pallett and colleagues found about 46 percent of face width was preferred on female faces and matched the average; the authors cautioned the sample was limited [10].

claims.claim: Wide-set or close-set eyes read differently by sex and face shape
claims.believers: Threads compare wide-set and close-set examples and ask whether attractive male figures have close-set eyes [6][19].
claims.experts: A 2026 preprint on male faces found preferred ratios near those reported for female faces, and the authors said no single universal optimum could be determined [11].
